models.summary: A quasi-Markov chain advances the colony one year at a time. The state is the count at each of 100 ages. Survival moves a cohort up one age and births, scaled by a constant 1.08, enter at age one; every other transition is zero. The scalar was chosen so the population grows and then settles near 18,100. Searching starting mixes shows that bringing no children produces a large retired share after about 40 years, so the chosen Population Zero puts 4,000 people evenly across ages 1 to 20 and 6,000 across ages 21 to 40, split evenly by gender. Occupations for the 6,000 working adults are sized by dimensional analysis: farming from calorie yield, health scaled by a traveler illness factor, and the rest from ratios and rates, giving 2,449 farmers.

models.summary: Years of schooling are tied to GDP per capita with Barro-Lee attainment data and World Bank income. A linear fit and a quadratic fit tie exactly, both with R-squared 0.27 and an Akaike score of 2710, so both are kept to bound a range. Child-labor rules force 9 years of general schooling. At the equilibrium population of 18,161, about 10,800 of the 11,264 working-age people have jobs, so roughly 464 continue to university, and 120 skilled openings a year make university last 3.87 years. The average student therefore spends 11.02 years in school, and the cautious linear projection gives a GDP of 289.613 million dollars.

models.summary: GDP is consumption plus investment plus government spending, with net exports set to zero because the colony cannot trade. Government pay falls across three tiers, set at 65 percent of US private-sector averages: 50,024.7, 40,696.5 and 25,260.3 dollars, while farmers and commerce workers keep the full 38,862. Each worker supports themselves and two thirds of a child, and food demand rises with salary above 2,000 kcal. Private investment is taken as negligible. Government spending on research, schooling and wages plus private spending on food and healthcare gives a GDP of 288.732 million dollars, against 289.613 million from the education model. The wage list gives a Gini coefficient of 0.0336 and a tax rate of 73.64 percent.
objectives: Reach a high GDP without a large wage gap.

models.summary: Five races move through jobs. Each year 5 percent of the workforce leaves, covering graduates, retirees and a few job changes. A mover prefers jobs holding more of their own race, scaled by a homophily factor of 1.2, chosen below the extremes in the cited network data. Segregation is the dissimilarity index: half the sum over jobs of the absolute gap between two races' shares. With equal pay, dissimilarity rises, because only contacts and taste drive the choice. Adding the tiered salaries pulls people toward higher pay and cuts dissimilarity, though not to zero. Gender policy is a shared six-month parental leave, watched through the same index.
models.purpose: Show that tiered pay reduces segregation.
objectives: Lower job segregation without giving up the wage ladder.

models.summary: The three models merge into one happiness index over four areas: schooling, efficiency, income equality and social equality. Schooling is years divided by 44, from Mincer. Efficiency is the colony's percentile in the Earth GDP-per-capita distribution, 0.76754. Income equality is one minus the Gini coefficient. Social equality is the harmonic mean of one minus each dissimilarity, 0.9287899, so one bad value pulls the score down. Weights come from the Pew Values Survey, scored 3, 2, 1, 0 and normalized, mapped from income slices onto the colony's tiers and recomputed by gender and by working versus retired. Flattening all wages drops the harmonic mean to 0.8894 and lowers happiness for every group, so the tiered pay stays.
